title: IUCN Red List of Ecosystem for the forest of the Americas
text:
This website provides a summary and update of the results from the IUCN Red List of Ecosystem (RLE) assessment for the tropical and temperate forests macrogroups of the Americas.
The original assessment and analysis was published by Ferrer-Paris et al. (2019).
The continental-scale assessment was a flagship project of the IUCN Red List of Ecosystem Thematic group and is used as an example for many other applications of the RLE (Bland et al. 2019; Nicholson et al. 2024). There is a critical need to update and improve the assessment as new information is available and make sure future users are aware of the caveats of this assessment and that they are able to use the best available data and results for decision making and reporting.
An official summary of the original assessment is available on-line, and the original results dataset (Rdata format) is available at:

Ferrer-Paris, José R. (2018): IUCN Red List of Ecosystem assessment results for IVC Forest Macrogroups in the Americas region. figshare. Dataset. https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.7488872.v1

Output of this dataset was also used to illustrate the application of Ecosystem indices in Rowland et al. (2019).




References

Bland, Lucie M., Emily Nicholson, Rebecca M. Miller, Angela Andrade, Aurélien Carré, Andres Etter, José Rafael Ferrer-Paris, et al. 2019. “Impacts of the IUCN Red List of Ecosystems on Conservation Policy and Practice.” Conservation Letters 12 (5): e12666. https://doi.org/10.1111/conl.12666.


Ferrer-Paris, José Rafael, Irene Zager, David A. Keith, María A. Oliveira-Miranda, Jon Paul Rodríguez, Carmen Josse, Mario González-Gil, Rebecca M. Miller, Carlos Zambrana-Torrelio, and Edmund Barrow. 2019. “An Ecosystem Risk Assessment of Temperate and Tropical Forests of the Americas with an Outlook on Future Conservation Strategies.” Conservation Letters 12 (2): e12623. https://doi.org/10.1111/conl.12623.


Nicholson, Emily, Angela Andrade, Amanda Driver, José R Ferrer-Paris, David Keith, Michael Sievers, and Simone Stevenson. 2024. “Beyond the Headline: Roles of the Red List of Ecosystems in Implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.” Nature Ecology and Evolution. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-023-02320-5.


Rowland, Jessica A., Lucie M. Bland, David A. Keith, Diego Juffe-Bignoli, Mark A. Burgman, Andres Etter, José Rafael Ferrer-Paris, Rebecca M. Miller, Andrew L. Skowno, and Emily Nicholson. 2019. “Ecosystem Indices to Support Global Biodiversity Conservation.” Conservation Letters 13 (1). https://doi.org/10.1111/conl.12680.

title: Bolivia
text:
There are subnational assessments for Bolivia (Maillard 2018).
There are interested organisations planning to do RLE assessments in Bolivia.
Local organisations should be contacted to enquire about the status of RLE assessments in the country.
Results from the continental assessment can be used for academic purposes. The results for this country should be considered preliminary until national assessments are completed, and should not be used for conservation planning and action without proper national level validation and consultation with relevant stakeholders.




References

Maillard, Ruth AND Vides-Almonacid, Oswaldo AND Anívarro. 2018. “Estado de conservación de los ecosistemas de las serranías chiquitanas: Un caso de estudio de la Lista Roja de Ecosistemas de la UICN en Bolivia.” Ecología En Bolivia 53 (September): 128–49. http://www.scielo.org.bo/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S1605-25282018000200005&nrm=iso.

title: This is how we built this site!
text:
This website was built to provide additional information about the continental assessment of forest in the Americas.
Information provided with the intention of improving documentation and encouraging appropriate use of the data, but we take no responsibility for errors of commission or omission.
Please consider that this website is under continuous destruction and reconstruction, but you should be able to access the historical records of changes by consulting the commit history in the GitHub repository. If you require clarifications about any changes, please open an issue or send me a message.

title: This is how we built this site!
section: We built this site with Rock-‘n’-Roll!
text:
We built this site with Rock-‘n’-Roll!
Not really, but appropriate background music helps a lot!
All files are available in a GitHub repository. The mostly-harmless branch uses Quarto to build the site.
Initialise a quarto website with:
cd ~/proyectos/IUCN-RLE/RLE-forests-panam-results
quarto create project website websrc
The source code of the website is in subfolder websrc but the output folder with the html content is defined in websrc/_quarto.yml.

title: This is how we built this site!
text:
Render site
With quarto and RStudio we can open the Build tab and select Build Website…
Or we can go to the command line and render the site:
quarto render websrc
And then launch a preview:
quarto preview websrc
If this work, we can just git add, git commit and git push it to the repo and see the changes!

title: This is how we built this site!
text:
Font Awesome
They work well out of the box with Rmarkdown, but for quarto we need to install an extension.
Switch to the repository folder and checkout the git branch we are working on, and then:
quarto install extension quarto-ext/fontawesome
Now I can use {{< fa smile >}} in the text and get a , or {{< fa lemon >}} and get a .

title: Chile
text:

Results from the continental assessment should only be used for academic purposes.

title: Chile
text:
National vegetation map
For Chile the current version of the map used for the national RLE assessment is available in Zenodo at https://zenodo.org/records/60800 (Luebert and Pliscoff 2017).

title: Chile
text:
National assessment

Download the data
The repository includes several compressed shapefiles and csv files with additional tabular data (check file shape_pisos.zip), and it also includes a csv file with the IUCN RLE results.
We first download and uncompress the shapefile with the vegetion units shape_pisos:
wget 'https://zenodo.org/record/60800/files/shape_pisos.zip?download=1' \
    -O shape_pisos.zip
unzip -u shape_pisos.zip
Then we download the csv file with the conservation status:
wget https://zenodo.org/record/60800/files/estado_conservacion.csv?download=1 \
    -O estado_conservacion.csv


Combine data
We need to combine the new table with the attribute table of the shapefile. One option is to use the functions in the gdal library to perform a join operation on the tables:
ogr2ogr \
    -sql "select CODIGO, PISO, FORMACION, Evaluación_Final from shape_pisos\
         left join 'estado_conservacion.csv'.estado_conservacion \
         on shape_pisos.CODIGO = estado_conservacion.Código_Piso" \ 
    Chile-RLE.gpkg shape_pisos.shp -nlt MULTIPOLYGON

title: Chile
text:
Visualise risk categories

First step: create map using gdal_rasterize
We can use other functions in the gdal library to transform the vector file we just created into a raster file with values of 1 to 6 for the RLE categories DD to CR:
LAYER=shape_pisos
OGRINPUT=Chile-RLE.gpkg
GDALOUTPUT=RLE-Chile-cat.tif 
CATCOLUMN=Evaluación_Final
gdal_rasterize -burn 0 -ts 500 1500 -l $LAYER $OGRINPUT $GDALOUTPUT
gdal_rasterize -burn 1 -where "$CATCOLUMN='DD'" -l $LAYER $OGRINPUT $GDALOUTPUT
gdal_rasterize -burn 2 -where "$CATCOLUMN='LC'" -l $LAYER $OGRINPUT $GDALOUTPUT
gdal_rasterize -burn 3 -where "$CATCOLUMN='NT'" -l $LAYER $OGRINPUT $GDALOUTPUT
gdal_rasterize -burn 4 -where "$CATCOLUMN='VU'" -l $LAYER $OGRINPUT $GDALOUTPUT
gdal_rasterize -burn 5 -where "$CATCOLUMN='EN'" -l $LAYER $OGRINPUT $GDALOUTPUT
gdal_rasterize -burn 6 -where "$CATCOLUMN='CR'" -l $LAYER $OGRINPUT $GDALOUTPUT


Second step: show map using R

here::i_am("systematic-assessments/Chile.qmd")
data_folder <- "Data"

library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyterra)
library(sf)

## country boundaries (World Bank source)
WB_file <- here::here(data_folder,
    "WB_Boundaries_GeoJSON_lowres/WB_countries_Admin0_lowres.geojson")
CHL_pol <- vect(sf::read_sf(WB_file)) %>% 
    filter(ISO_A3 %in% "CHL")

clrs <- c(
  "NE" = "white",
  "DD" = "grey",
  "LC" = "green4",
  "NT" = "green",
  "VU" = "yellow",
  "EN" = "orange",
  "CR" = "red")

CHL <- rast(here::here(data_folder, "RLE-Chile-cat.tif"))
levels(CHL) <- data.frame(val=0:6,cat=c("NE","DD","LC","NT","VU","EN","CR"))

plot(CHL, col=clrs[c(1,3,5,6,7)], 
    main = CHL_pol$FORMAL_EN, 
    legend = TRUE, axes = TRUE,)
plot(CHL_pol, add = T)

Compare this with published maps, for example this one.
